CausalChain: Chronic inflammation in the liver → HCC cell metabolic reprogramming → Increased production of SAM and MTA → Epigenetic remodeling in infiltrating T cells (upregulation of PD-1/TIM-3) → T cell exhaustion → Impaired anti-tumor immunity → Enhanced tumor progression
Hypothesis: Inhibition of methionine adenosyltransferase in HCC cells will reduce SAM/MTA production, thereby restoring T cell effector function in the TME and enhancing the response to immunotherapy in hepatocellular carcinoma.
Abstract: Chronic liver inflammation in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) not only remodels the tumor microenvironment (TME) by recruiting immune and stromal cells but also drives metabolic reprogramming in tumor cells that contributes to immune suppression. Notably, HCC cells exhibit enhanced synthesis of methionine metabolites—such as S‐adenosylmethionine (SAM) and methylthioadenosine (MTA)—which have been implicated in altering T cell chromatin landscapes and promoting the expression of inhibitory receptors, leading to T cell exhaustion. This review integrates findings regarding cytokine signaling, metabolic alterations, and immune checkpoint expression within the TME. We propose that targeting the methionine cycle, specifically through inhibition of methionine adenosyltransferase, may reduce SAM/MTA levels in the TME, reverse epigenetic modifications in T cells, reinvigorate their cytotoxic function, and ultimately improve the efficacy of immunotherapeutic strategies in HCC. Such an approach could offer a combinatorial regimen to overcome therapy resistance in this aggressive malignancy.
